prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 1, the first notebook of part 1 (regression on hourly bike rentals) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: tabular foundation models (TFMs) bring the idea of a pretrained large language model answering from a prompt to tables. TabICL's transformer was pretrained once, on millions of synthetic tables, and predicts new rows by reading our training rows as context. The data is hourly bike rentals (target `count`); `season`, `holiday`, `workingday` and `weather` are categorical. The notebook explains why `cv=5` (a non-shuffled KFold) would train on the future for every fold but the last, and uses `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=10, gap=48, max_train_size=800, test_size=200)`, capped at 800 rows because a longer context costs TabICL more compute.

A note before the setup cells explains that the notebooks call TabICL through TabAPI so that they run in a browser, and that students running locally should prefer the `tabicl` package. Section 'What fit does for TabICL' describes the local package: `fit` trains nothing, it loads the weights and stores the rows, and the first call downloads about 110 MB of weights. Through TabAPI, `fit` makes no network call, so both `%%time` cells are near-instant; if a student notices this, explain that the text describes the local package.

Results of the reference run: with default hyperparameters (TabICL with its default 8 ensemble members), TabICL's MAE is about 37 bikes per hour against 42 for HGBT, with wide boxes because some folds fall in unusually quiet or busy stretches. HGBT spends its time in `fit`, TabICL in `predict` (several seconds for 200 rows with 800 context rows on a laptop). A `RandomizedSearchCV` over HGBT's tree-complexity hyperparameters, with a nested `TimeSeriesSplit` inside each training fold and budgets `n_iter` nested thanks to `random_state`, does not beat TabICL: one candidate is worse than the defaults, 8 candidates match them, 16 bring no further gain (about 42) while fit time more than doubles. At `n_iter=8`, HGBT spends about as much compute as TabICL.

Place in the course: first notebook. Next come exercise 1 on `n_estimators` (ensemble members, introduced here only as 'default hyperparameters'), then the learning curve. Questions on later topics (ensemble members, learning curves, missing values, prediction intervals, calibration, decision thresholds) get a brief answer and a pointer to the notebook that covers them. Related scikit-learn course material: time series cross-validation and randomized search (Evaluating Model Performance; Hyperparameter Tuning), histogram gradient boosting (Ensemble Models).
